newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian parties seek end to election row crisis.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parties seek end to election row crisis.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was trying to thrash out a compromise between political parties on Monday over planned elections regarded as vital to stop the country plunging back into chaos.
"We will try to decide something...today," Fino said during a break in talks with the parties of his national unity government, most of which have threatened to boycott the June 29 vote.
The parties say election rules favour President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.

The elections aim to restore stability to Albania and prevent a repeat of the unrest of February and March, when people left penniless by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes took to the streets in an orgy of looting.
A spokesman for Fino said the parties met for two hours in the morning and would assemble again in the afternoon.
Fino leads a nine-party Government of National Reconciliation, which Berisha was forced to install in March to calm the population.
"The aim of the prime minister is to...create a group of compromise amendments," the spokesman said.
Fino will either recall parliament to pass the amendments or ask Berisha to sign decrees to bring them into force, he added.
As the politicians haggled, Albania suffered sporadic bouts of violence, fuelled by the million or so weapons looted from state arsenals.
Police said seven people had been killed overnight on Sunday, including two in the southern port town of Vlore who were murdered by masked gunmen at a cafe.

Frightened residents of Vlore, at the heart of the March lawlessness, refused to send their children to school although armoured vehicles of the Italian-led multinational force, which is protecting aid supplies, were patrolling the town.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel kept up constant Western pressure for a compromise as he spoke with Fino by telephone late on Sunday.
"This is in the interests of the Albanians and of the international community, which is committed to help Albania overcome the crisis," state-run news agency ATA quoted Kinkel as telling Fino.
Kinkel's warning was the latest of a series of statements from Western governments urging compromise.
The European Union, Italy and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have said they may withdraw aid unless free and fair elections go ahead.
Italy, which leads the multinational force has said the troops may pull out if the elections fail.
Parties against the election law want the government and not the president to be in charge of administering the polls.
They have also asked that the government names the electoral commission, seek changes in voting districts and a legal definition of the status of international monitors.
In the last elections in 1996, the Socialists pulled out on the last day. The international community wants to avoid a repeat of that poll, which the OSCE described as deeply flawed.
